conflict_topics: National Day leave scheduling (who works which of the two days)
conditional offers / reciprocity (C's offer contingent on Christmas cover)
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants propose concrete, testable staffing plans rather than abstract statements ('if I work the first day...' — Turn 9).
Agent C consistently links two separate scheduling issues (National Day and Christmas), which is the key structural tension.
There is clear turn-taking and role clarity; statements remain on-topic and reference prior offers, making the dialogue highly grounded.
evaluation.final_reason: No mutual agreement remained at the end. Although Agent B volunteered to cover Christmas (Turn 21) and Agents A and B proposed a National Day plan (A works the first day, B the second), Agent C rejected the implied consequence that he would work both National Day dates and insisted his offer was to work one day only ('I offered to work one day, not two.'). That refusal was not accommodated and no alternative compromise was accepted, so the substantive incompatibility remained unresolved.
position_change_notes: Agent B amended their need early (Turn 4): from initially asking both days off to being available on the second day only.
Agent A shifted from requesting leave to proposing to work the first National Day (Turns 7–9) — a partial concession to resolve the National Day conflict.
Agent C retained the core position that his offer was for one day only and conditioned it on Christmas cover; he did not accept the plan that would require two days of work.
Agent D remained firm about being unable to work Christmas and retained the need for both National Day days off.

round_scores.evidence: Agent A: '...three of us have asked for those two days off.' Agent B: 'My son's childcare is closed on both those days.' (Incompatible leave requests identified.)

Agent A: '...my whole family has a trip to Malaysia planned for those days.' Agent B: 'My mother can look after him on the second day. It's the first day I have no one.' (B reduces need to one day, lowering immediate incompatibility.)

Agent C conditions an offer: 'I'll work one of these National Day holidays if someone covers Christmas for me.' Agent D: 'I can't do Christmas. And I need both those days off. It's my sister's wedding.' (Introduces a linked conflict across two rostering issues and an explicit refusal to provide the requested cover.)

Agent A offers a concrete compromise for National Day: 'I might be able to work the first day and join my family late.' Agent B accepts. (Partial solution for National Day, but C's Christmas condition remains.)

Agent A outlines a staffing plan that would require Agent C to work both National Day dates without C's agreement: '...then on the second day, I'm off and Agent D is off, so Agent B, you'd work that day?' Agent B: 'Yes.' (Plan created but relies on C accepting extra work.)
Agent D affirms the proposed National Day arrangement: 'Yeah, that works perfectly.' (Removes one obstacle, but C's conditional offer and Christmas cover still unresolved.)

Agent C: 'Hold on. That works for the three of you. But that doesn't solve the roster. What about Christmas?' Agent D: 'You're right, that still needs to be sorted. But I really can't work on Christmas.' (C restates the condition; D reiterates refusal — linkage remains contested.)

Agent C: 'Okay, so Agent D can't. What about one of you? I've worked the last two Christmases.' Agent A proposes locking in the National Day plan first, but C objects to separating the issues. (Disagreement about whether to treat the two problems together.)

Agent C: 'No. We sort them out together. My offer to work is for a Christmas cover. If that doesn't happen, the National Day roster isn't settled.' Agent A agrees to sort Christmas next. (C maintains the conditionality; conflict persists.)

Agent B: 'I can work Christmas.' Agent A summarizes: B covers Christmas; National Day: A works first, B works second. (A concrete settlement is offered, but C has not yet accepted whether this forces him to work both National Day dates.)

Agent C: '...your plan for National Day has me working both days. I offered to work one day, not two.' Agent A: 'You're right, that's what you offered. But on the first day... it has to be me and you working. And on the second day... it has to be Agent B and you.' (Explicit incompatible expectations about who must work.)

Agent C: 'So because everyone else's plans are fixed, I have to work both days. That wasn't the offer.' Agent B: 'He's right. He said he'd work one day, not two.' (Positions are entrenched: C insists he offered one day; others treat the plan as forcing him to cover both.)

substantive_insights: C's willingness to work one National Day is explicitly conditional on someone covering Christmas; treating the issues separately undermines that condition.
Changing one person's availability (B reducing to one day) materially shifts feasible assignments and creates a situation where C would be asked to do more than he offered.
There are hard constraints (D cannot work Christmas; A has family travel but can delay arrival one day) that limit feasible compromises and make some reassignment unattractive or impossible.
